reasoning: The quote is verbatim (ms3 transcript line 1051, Q1 teaching point). But the finding's central DSM claim is itself wrong: DSM-5-TR names hospitalization in BOTH places — Criterion A carries the duration exception ('lasting at least 1 week and present most of the day, nearly every day (or any duration if hospitalization is necessary)') and Criterion C independently lists it as a severity outcome ('sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment ... or to necessitate hospitalization ..., or there are psychotic features'). So the page's 'causing marked impairment, hospitalization, or psychotic features' is a faithful rendering of Criterion C, not a misfiling of the duration exception, and the finding's framing ('the hospitalisation clause IS the duration exception, not one of several severity outcomes') would teach a new error if pasted in. What survives, and is worth fixing, is the omission: the bare '≥1 week' drops both the duration exception and 'most of the day, nearly every day', while the page's own facilitator note (line 1102) states the rule fully ('mania ≥1 week (or any duration if hospitalized)') — learner text diverging from its own answer key, which is exactly the S2 'rationale that contradicts its own keyed answer'. The reviewer also overreads the stem: four days of observed behaviour change with roughly a week of reduced sleep is ambiguous, not clearly sub-week, so the replacement must not assert that the exception is the only route by which this patient meets criteria. Severity S2 stands; problem statement and replacement corrected below.

corrected_finding.quote: DSM criteria for mania require **≥1 week** of persistently elevated/irritable mood **plus increased activity/energy** and ≥3 symptoms (≥4 if mood is only irritable), causing marked impairment, hospitalization, or psychotic features.
corrected_finding.problem: The Criterion C half of this sentence is fine — DSM-5-TR does list marked impairment, necessitating hospitalization, or psychotic features as alternative severity outcomes. The defect is in the duration half: '≥1 week' is stated bare, dropping both 'present most of the day, nearly every day' and, more importantly, Criterion A's duration exception ('or any duration if hospitalization is necessary'). The page's own facilitator notes state the rule completely ('mania ≥1 week (or any duration if hospitalized)'), so the learner-facing text and the answer key say different things. It matters for this stem: the roommate describes four days of behaviour change with about a week of reduced sleep, so the episode's start date is genuinely ambiguous, and a student applying a bare one-week rule can talk themselves out of a case the same paragraph calls 'a classic manic episode'. The same student will then reject mania in the hospitalized patient symptomatic for four days — a common real presentation and a common shelf item.
corrected_finding.replacement: DSM criteria for mania require a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood **plus abnormally increased goal-directed activity or energy**, lasting **≥1 week and present most of the day, nearly every day — or any duration if hospitalization is necessary** — with ≥3 associated symptoms (≥4 if mood is only irritable), and causing marked impairment, necessitating hospitalization, or with psychotic features. Note that hospitalization does double duty in the criteria: it satisfies the duration requirement at *any* duration, and it also counts as a severity outcome — so a patient admitted on day four of clear mania meets criteria even if you cannot pin the episode to a full week.
corrected_finding.basis: DSM-5-TR, Bipolar I Disorder, Manic Episode Criterion A (duration, with the hospitalization exception) and Criterion C (severity: marked impairment, necessitates hospitalization, or psychotic features); and this page's own facilitator note, 'mania ≥1 week (or any duration if hospitalized)'.

corrected_finding.quote: **Thiamine parenterally, before dextrose** [12]. Replete **magnesium** and potassium.
corrected_finding.problem: The page flags Wernicke encephalopathy prominently and correctly — differential table ('classic triad present in a minority — most cases are missed'), ranked differential ('treat empirically; do not wait for the triad'), and 'before any dextrose' — but across all four mentions it gives only route and sequence, never distinguishing prophylactic from treatment dosing. That is the distinction that changes management: the order a resident writes by reflex is thiamine 100 mg IV daily, which is a prophylaxis dose and does not treat suspected WE in a malnourished, delirious patient. The page cites a review whose entire subject is how widely guideline thiamine regimens differ [12] without naming that a treatment indication exists at all, so the learner has no cue that the protocol they are being sent to has two different answers in it. Same paragraph, second gap: magnesium is listed as repletion housekeeping rather than as the reason thiamine may not work — Mg 1.4 in this stem is an uncorrected cofactor deficiency.
corrected_finding.replacement: **Thiamine parenterally, before dextrose** — and note that this is a *treatment* indication, not prophylaxis: suspected Wernicke encephalopathy calls for high-dose parenteral thiamine, given several times daily for the first days and then tapered to a lower parenteral course, per your institutional protocol. The reflexive once-daily order most of us write is a prophylactic dose and does not treat WE; guideline regimens for the treatment indication vary substantially, which is itself the subject of [12], so read the protocol rather than reaching for the familiar number. Replete **magnesium** and potassium — magnesium is an obligate cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes, so thiamine will underperform until his magnesium of 1.4 is corrected.
corrected_finding.basis: Guideline thiamine regimens separate a treatment indication for suspected/established WE (EFNS 2010: 200 mg tds IV; UK RCP/BAP-derived practice commonly 500 mg tds for 2-3 days, then a reduced parenteral course) from a prophylaxis indication in high-risk AUD inpatients at a substantially lower daily dose. The page's own ref [12] (Pruckner 2019, Eur Addict Res, https://doi.org/10.1159/000499039) reviewed 14 guidelines and found application modality, indication, and dose recommendations varied considerably, with several giving no dose at all — which is why the distinction, not a single number, is what belongs on the page. Magnesium is a cofactor for transketolase and other thiamine-pyrophosphate-dependent enzymes; refractory WE with uncorrected hypomagnesaemia is described. Note the page's closing convention ('Specific dosing is intentionally omitted; follow your institution's protocol and consult pharmacy') — if the author prefers explicit mg figures here, that disclaimer must be amended in the same edit.

Quote verbatim at resident transcript line 650. The reading is fair, not strict: the clause sits under a bolded 'Liver caveat:', and the antecedent of 'a real reason' is the immediately preceding HE clause, so the sentence does convert sedative-precipitated hepatic encephalopathy into an affirmative argument FOR phenobarbital, in the same breath as recommending lorazepam/oxazepam. The pharmacology is correct: phenobarbital is largely hepatically metabolised (CYP2C9), its adult elimination half-life is already on the order of 80-120 h and is further prolonged in hepatic impairment, there is no reversal agent, and as a potent sedative it can precipitate HE exactly as benzodiazepines can — hepatic impairment argues for more caution with a barbiturate load, not less. The citation check the finding itself invited comes out in its favour: according to PubMed, ref [7] (Chand 2022, J Clin Exp Hepatol, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jceh.2022.03.003) concludes that 'Lorazepam and oxazepam are preferred agents for the management of AWS in the setting of ALD' and that 'In severe ALD, benzodiazepines should be used cautiously with monitoring due to the risk of excessive sedation or precipitating hepatic encephalopathy' — it supports the first half of the page's sentence and offers nothing endorsing barbiturate loading in alcohol-related liver disease, so the citation is mis-attached to the conclusion it is hung on. The replacement is correct and relocates the phenobarbital rationale to benzodiazepine resistance, which this page's Q4 establishes well, so it does not accidentally argue phenobarbital out of a patient who needs it. S2 ('wrong mechanism') is right — the drug choice is defensible here, only the hepatic rationale is wrong. Minor, not enough to downgrade: the 'no reversal agent' point carries little practical weight, since flumazenil is not used in alcohol withdrawal either; the substantive half of that argument is the multi-day half-life.

corrected_finding.quote: Hypercalcemia can itself produce confusion and contributes to nephrogenic DI. Two lithium effects converging.
corrected_finding.problem: A corrected calcium of 10.9 mg/dL is mild hypercalcaemia, well below the range at which hypercalcaemia produces neuropsychiatric depression of consciousness — obtundation is generally a feature above roughly 12-13 mg/dL and frank encephalopathy above about 14. Offering it as a contributor to this delirium supplies a false alternative explanation for an encephalopathy the page correctly assigns to chronic lithium neurotoxicity, and teaches the resident to attribute causal weight to a lab value that does not carry it. The error is asserted at three loci and all three need the fix: this Q3 differential entry; the summary line '**Hypercalcemic encephalopathy** from lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism — *concurrent contributor*', ranked #3, above uraemic/metabolic encephalopathy at #5; and — most consequentially, because it is the answer key — facilitator common-error #6, which tells the facilitator that not connecting the hypercalcaemia to lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism means 'missing a treatable contributor to both the encephalopathy and the polyuria'. Her concentrating defect is separately and better explained by lithium itself, as this page's own Q4 teaches (ENaC entry into collecting-duct principal cells, impaired AQP2), so hypercalcaemia should not be doing explanatory work for the polyuria either.
corrected_finding.replacement: Her corrected calcium of 10.9 with an inappropriately elevated PTH is real and is lithium's doing, but read it as a *marker* of lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism (Q6) rather than as a contributor to tonight's picture: mild hypercalcaemia at this level does not produce encephalopathy — that generally requires >12-13 mg/dL — and her concentrating defect is already fully accounted for by lithium's direct effect on the collecting duct (Q4). Two lithium effects converging, but only one of them is driving the neurologic picture. [Apply the same correction to the summary differential — demote the hypercalcaemia line below uraemic/metabolic encephalopathy and relabel it 'marker of lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism, not a driver of the encephalopathy' — and to facilitator common-error #6, where the point to teach is connecting the hypercalcaemia to lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism as a monitorable endocrine effect requiring follow-up, not as a treatable contributor to the encephalopathy.]
corrected_finding.basis: Standard thresholds for symptomatic hypercalcaemia: mild (roughly 10.5-12 mg/dL) is usually asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic; neuropsychiatric features and obtundation belong to the moderate-to-severe range (about 12-14 mg/dL and above), with hypercalcaemic crisis above that. Endocrine Society primary-hyperparathyroidism guidance and standard internal-medicine teaching on hypercalcaemia. Hypercalcaemia-induced nephrogenic DI (calcium-sensing-receptor-mediated AQP2 downregulation) likewise requires higher calcium levels than this; the page's own Q4 attributes her concentrating defect to lithium via ENaC and AQP2.
